prompt: A classifier is evaluated on 1,000 cases: TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 930. What are its precision and recall?

options.explanation: These are swapped. Precision divides by predicted positives (TP + FP = 50); recall divides by actual positives (TP + FN = 60).
Correct. Precision = 40/50 = 0.80; recall = 40/60 ≈ 0.67.
0.97 is the accuracy, (40 + 930)/1000. It is inflated by the 930 easy true negatives.
0.04 is TP divided by all 1,000 cases, which isn't a standard metric. Precision only looks at the cases the model flagged.

workedExample:
```
           pred +   pred -
actual +   TP 40    FN 20   (60)
actual -   FP 10    TN 930
          (50)
```

1. Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 40 / 50 = **0.80**. Of 50 alerts, 40 were real.
2. Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 40 / 60 ≈ **0.67**. Of 60 real cases, 40 were caught.
3. F1 = 2 × 0.8 × 0.667 / 1.467 ≈ 0.73.
4. Accuracy is 0.97, which sounds great but says nothing about the 20 missed cases.

prompt: A screening test flags patients for a follow-up scan. Missing a real case can be fatal; a false alarm costs one extra scan. Which metric should you prioritise?

options.explanation: Precision measures how many alerts are real, which matters when false alarms are costly. Here false alarms are cheap; misses are the expensive error.
With a rare disease, accuracy is dominated by healthy patients and can be high while many cases are missed.
Specificity is the share of healthy patients correctly cleared. It is about avoiding false alarms, which is the cheaper error here.
Correct. Recall = TP / (TP + FN) directly measures the share of real cases caught, which is what a screening test must maximise.

workedExample:
1. List the errors: a **false negative** (missed case) is potentially fatal; a **false positive** costs a scan.
2. The metric that falls when false negatives rise is recall = TP / (TP + FN).
3. So set a low threshold and aim for high recall, accepting lower precision.
4. If you need one number that leans this way, use F2, which weights recall more than precision.

prompt: A model has ROC-AUC = 0.80. What does that mean?

options.text: If you pick one positive and one negative at random, there is an 80% chance the positive gets the higher score
options.explanation: Correct. ROC-AUC equals the probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative.
AUC doesn't depend on a threshold, while accuracy does. A model with AUC 0.80 can have almost any accuracy depending on where you cut.

options.text: 80% of the model's alerts are correct
options.explanation: That describes precision at some threshold, which AUC doesn't measure.
That is recall at one particular threshold. AUC summarises all thresholds.

workedExample:
1. ROC-AUC is the area under the TPR-vs-FPR curve across all thresholds.
2. Equivalently, count every (positive, negative) pair and check whether the positive scored higher (ties count half).
3. AUC = correctly ordered pairs / all pairs. In the lesson's 12-example set: 30 / 35 ≈ 0.857.
4. So 0.80 means 80% of pairs are ranked correctly. 0.5 is coin-flipping; 1.0 is perfect ranking.

link.title: Classification: ROC and AUC — Google ML Crash Course

prompt: A model has precision 0.9 and recall 0.3. What is its F1 score?

options.explanation: That is the arithmetic mean. F1 is the harmonic mean, which is pulled towards the smaller value.
That is the product P × R. F1 = 2PR / (P + R).
F1 is pulled towards the minimum but isn't equal to it unless P = R or one is 0.

workedExample:
F1 = 2PR / (P + R)

```
2 × 0.9 × 0.3 = 0.54
0.9 + 0.3     = 1.20
F1 = 0.54/1.2 = 0.45
```

The arithmetic mean would be 0.60, hiding the fact that 70% of positives are missed. The harmonic mean punishes this lopsidedness, which is the point of using it.

prompt:
Compute the ROC-AUC by counting pairs.

```
positive scores: 0.9, 0.6, 0.4
negative scores: 0.7, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1
```

options.explanation: That would be 9 correct of 12. Recount: only the pairs (0.6, 0.7) and (0.4, 0.7) are wrong, so 10 are correct.
Correct. 3 × 4 = 12 pairs; 10 have the positive above the negative, so AUC = 10/12 ≈ 0.833.
That is 2/3, perhaps the share of positives above 0.5. AUC counts positive–negative pairs.
That is 11/12, missing one of the two misordered pairs. Both 0.6 and 0.4 are below the negative at 0.7.

workedExample:
For each positive, count how many negatives it beats:

```
0.9 beats 0.7 0.3 0.2 0.1 -> 4
0.6 beats     0.3 0.2 0.1 -> 3
0.4 beats     0.3 0.2 0.1 -> 3
                     total   10
```

Pairs = 3 × 4 = 12. AUC = 10 / 12 ≈ 0.833.

Note that only the ranking matters: replacing every score by its square would give the same AUC.

prompt: True delivery times are 10, 12, 15, 20 minutes; the model predicts 11, 12, 13, 26. What are the MAE and RMSE?

options.explanation: 1.25 is the mean *signed* error (1 + 0 − 2 + 6)/4, where positives and negatives cancel. MAE uses absolute values.
10.25 is the MSE. RMSE is its square root, which brings it back to minutes.
Correct. Absolute errors 1, 0, 2, 6 average 2.25; squared errors 1, 0, 4, 36 average 10.25, and √10.25 ≈ 3.20.
These are swapped. RMSE is always ≥ MAE, because squaring gives extra weight to the large errors.

workedExample:
Errors ŷ − y: 1, 0, −2, 6.

```
|e|: 1 0 2 6   sum 9   MAE = 2.25
e² : 1 0 4 36  sum 41  MSE = 10.25
RMSE = √10.25 ≈ 3.20
```

RMSE is noticeably above MAE because one error (6 minutes) dominates the squares: 36 of the 41. The bigger the gap between RMSE and MAE, the more your error is concentrated in a few large misses.

prompt:
Using the lesson's 12-example dataset, a missed positive costs £500 and a false alarm costs £5. Which threshold gives the lowest total cost?

| Threshold | TP | FP |
|---|---|---|
| 0.50 | 3 | 1 |
| 0.42 | 4 | 1 |
| 0.30 | 5 | 3 |
| 0.15 | 5 | 4 |

options.text: 0.50, because it has the fewest false alarms
options.explanation: It ties for fewest false alarms, but it misses 2 positives at £500 each: £1,005 in total.

options.text: 0.42, because it has the best F1
options.explanation: F1 weights the two errors equally. With misses costing 100 times more, cost (£505 here) is what matters.
Correct. No misses and 3 false alarms: 3 × £5 = £15, the lowest.
It catches no extra positives (all 5 were caught at 0.30) and adds a false alarm, so cost rises to £20.

workedExample:
Cost = FN × £500 + FP × £5, with FN = 5 − TP.

```
t     FN  FP   cost
0.50   2   1   1000+5  = 1005
0.42   1   1    500+5  =  505
0.30   0   3      15   =   15
0.15   0   4      20   =   20
```

The best threshold by F1 (0.42) is not the best by business cost. Choose thresholds on validation data using the real costs, then check the result on test.

prompt: You are detecting a defect that occurs in 0.1% of parts. Which metrics are informative for comparing models? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Predicting "no defect" for every part scores 99.9%. Accuracy can't separate a useless model from a good one here.
Correct. PR metrics focus on the rare positive class and react strongly to false positives, which dominate when positives are rare.

options.text: Recall at a fixed, acceptable number of alerts per day
options.explanation: Correct. This mirrors how the system is operated: inspectors can check N parts a day, so how many defects are in the top N?
Correct. It tells you what fraction of inspector time is spent on real defects.

workedExample:
1. At 0.1% prevalence, a do-nothing model has 99.9% accuracy, so accuracy is out.
2. ROC-AUC is not useless, but FPR divides by the huge negative count, so many false alarms barely move it. PR curves show them clearly.
3. A random classifier's AP equals the prevalence, 0.001, so even AP = 0.2 is a 200-fold lift.
4. Operational metrics (recall in the top N alerts, precision at the threshold) map directly onto inspector workload and missed defects, which is what the business actually feels.

prompt: A model predicts P(y = 1) for three examples: (y = 1, p = 0.9), (y = 0, p = 0.2), (y = 1, p = 0.4). What is the log loss (natural log)?

options.explanation: That uses log base 10. Log loss is conventionally defined with the natural log, which gives about 0.415.
That is the sum (0.105 + 0.223 + 0.916). Log loss is the mean over examples.
That uses −ln(0.2) for the negative example. For y = 0 you score the probability given to the true class, 1 − p = 0.8.

workedExample:
For each example, take −ln(probability assigned to the true class):

```
y=1, p=0.9: −ln(0.9) = 0.105
y=0, p=0.2: −ln(0.8) = 0.223
y=1, p=0.4: −ln(0.4) = 0.916
             sum     = 1.245
             mean    = 0.415
```

The third example dominates: it gave the true class only 40%. Had it said 0.01, that term alone would be −ln(0.01) ≈ 4.6. Log loss rewards calibrated, honest confidence.

prompt: A colleague replaces each predicted probability p with p² before evaluation (all p are between 0 and 1). Which metrics are guaranteed to be **unchanged**? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Squaring is strictly increasing on [0, 1], so every pair keeps its order, and AUC depends only on the order.
Correct. AP also depends only on the ranking of examples, which is unchanged.
Log loss uses the probability values themselves. Squaring pushes them down (0.8 becomes 0.64), which changes every term.
A case with p = 0.6 drops to 0.36 and falls below the threshold, so the confusion matrix at 0.5 changes. (The same results would appear at threshold 0.25.)

workedExample:
1. p ↦ p² is monotonic increasing on [0, 1]: if a > b then a² > b².
2. **Ranking metrics** (ROC-AUC, AP) see only the order, so they are unchanged.
3. **Threshold metrics** change unless you move the threshold too: threshold 0.5 on p² equals threshold √0.5 ≈ 0.707 on p.
4. **Probability metrics** (log loss, calibration) change, because the numbers themselves change.

This is why a model can have great AUC and terrible calibration: ranking and probability quality are separate properties.

prompt: A support-ticket router has 3 classes: Billing (800 tickets), Technical (180) and Legal (20). It gets every Billing and Technical ticket right but labels all Legal tickets as Billing. What are its accuracy and macro-F1?

options.explanation: Correct. Legal's F1 is 0, Technical's is 1.0, and Billing's is about 0.99, so the macro average is about 0.66 while accuracy is 0.98.
That is micro-F1, which equals accuracy for single-label problems. Macro-F1 averages per-class F1, so Legal's 0 drags it down.
Accuracy counts tickets, not classes: 980 of 1,000 are right.
Only Legal's F1 is 0; the other two classes score highly.

workedExample:
1. Accuracy = (800 + 180) / 1000 = 0.98.
2. Billing: TP 800, FP 20 (the Legal tickets), FN 0. P = 800/820 ≈ 0.976, R = 1. F1 ≈ 0.988.
3. Technical: P = R = 1. F1 = 1.
4. Legal: TP 0, so F1 = 0.
5. Macro-F1 = (0.988 + 1 + 0) / 3 ≈ 0.66.

If Legal tickets matter (they often do), macro-F1 or the per-class report exposes the failure that accuracy hides.

prompt: You add many more easy negatives to a test set (scored low by the model), increasing negatives tenfold while keeping positives the same. What happens to ROC-AUC and average precision?

options.text: Both stay the same, since the model hasn't changed
options.explanation: The model is the same, but AP depends on how many negatives sit above each positive, which can change with the negative pool.

options.text: Both fall, because the data is more imbalanced
options.explanation: ROC-AUC doesn't depend on class balance as such; it depends on the pairwise ordering.

options.text: ROC-AUC tends to rise; AP changes little, because the new negatives rank below every positive
options.explanation: Correct. Each easy negative adds pairs the model gets right, lifting AUC, but negatives below all positives don't change precision at any positive's rank.
Adding correctly ranked negatives can only add correct pairs, so AUC can't fall.

workedExample:
1. **AUC** = correct pairs / all pairs. Every new low-scoring negative forms a correct pair with every positive, so AUC moves towards 1. Padding a test set with easy negatives inflates AUC.
2. **AP** averages precision at each positive's rank. If the new negatives all rank below the lowest positive, no positive gains extra negatives above it, so AP is unchanged.
3. Contrast the lesson's example, where the duplicated negatives were *interleaved* with positives: AUC stayed 0.857 (same pairs, same ratios) but AP fell from 0.835 to about 0.53.

Lesson: AUC can be gamed by easy negatives; AP reflects how crowded the top of the ranking is.
